source_text: Κατορθωμάτων τε γὰρ τιμωμένων, ἀδικηθήσεται τὸ σῶμα σαφῶς ἐκ τοῦ κοινωνῆσαι μὲν τῇ ψυχῇ τῶν ἐπὶ τοῖς σπουδαζομένοις πόνων, μὴ κοινωνῆσαι δὲ τῆς ἐπὶ τοῖς κατορθωθεῖσι τιμῆς, καὶ συγγνώμης μὲν τυγχάνειν πολλάκις τὴν ψυχὴν ἐπί τινων πλημμελημάτων διὰ τὴν τοῦ σώματος ἔνδειάν τε καὶ χρείαν, ἐκπίπτειν δὲ αὐτὸ τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἐπὶ τοῖς κατορθωθεῖσι κοινωνίας, ὑπὲρ ὧν τοὺς ἐν τῇ ζωῇ συνδιήνεγκε πόνους. Καὶ μὴν καὶ πλημμελημάτων κρινομένων οὐ σώζεται τῇ ψυχῇ τὸ δίκαιον, εἴ γε μόνη τίνοι δίκην ὑπὲρ ὧν ἐνοχλοῦντος τοῦ σώματος καὶ πρὸς τὰς οἰκείας ὀρέξεις ἢ κινήσεις ἕλκοντος ἐπλημμέλησεν, ποτὲ μὲν κατὰ συναρπαγὴν καὶ κλοπήν, ποτὲ δὲ κατά τινα βιαιοτέραν ὁλκήν, ἄλλοτε δὲ κατὰ συνδρομὴν ἐν χάριτος μέρει καὶ θεραπείας τῆς τούτου συστάσεως. Ἢ πῶς οὐκ ἄδικον τὴν ψυχὴν κρίνεσθαι καθ᾿ ἑαυτὴν ὑπὲρ ὧν οὐδ᾿ ἡντινοῦν ἔχει κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτῆς φύσιν οὐκ ὄρεξιν, οὐ κίνησιν, οὐχ ὁρμήν, οἷον λαγνείας ἢ βίας ἢ πλεονεξίας ἢ ἀδικίας καὶ τῶν ἐπὶ τούτοις ἀδικημάτων; Εἰ γὰρ τὰ πλεῖστα τῶν τοιούτων γίνεται κακῶν ἐκ τοῦ μὴ κατακρατεῖν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τῶν ἐνοχλούντων παθῶν, ἐνοχλοῦνται δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ σώματος ἐνδείας καὶ χρείας καὶ τῆς περὶ τοῦτο σπουδῆς καὶ θεραπείας (τούτων γὰρ ἕνεκεν πᾶσα ἡ κτῆσις καὶ πρὸ ταύτης ἡ χρῆσις, ἔτι δὲ γάμος καὶ ὅσαι κατὰ τὸν βίον πράξεις, ἐν οἷς καὶ περὶ ἃ θεωρεῖται τό τε πλημμελὲς καὶ τὸ μὴ τοιοῦτον), ποῦ δίκαιον, ἐν οἷς πρωτοπαθεῖ τὸ σῶμα καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν ἕλκει πρὸς συμπάθειαν καὶ κοινωνίαν τῶν ἐφ᾿ ἃ δεῖται πράξεων, αὐτὴν κρίνεσθαι μόνην, καὶ τὰς μὲν ὀρέξεις καὶ τὰς ἡδονάς, ἔτι δὲ φόβους καὶ λύπας, ἐφ᾿ ὧν πᾶν τὸ μὴ μέτριον ὑπόδικον, ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος ἔχειν τὴν κίνησιν, τὰς δὲ ἐκ τούτων ἁμαρτίας καὶ τὰς ἐπὶ τοῖς ἡμαρτημένοις τιμωρίας ἐπὶ τὴν ψυχὴν φέρεσθαι μόνην, τὴν μήτε δεομένην τοιούτου τινὸς μήτε ὀρεγομένην μήτε φοβουμένην ἢ πάσχουσάν τι τοιοῦτον καθ᾿ ἑαυτὴν οἷον πάσχειν πέφυκεν ἄνθρωπος; Ἀλλὰ κἂν μὴ μόνου τοῦ σώματος, ἀνθρώπου δὲ θῶμεν εἶναι τὰ πάθη, λέγοντες ὀρθῶς διὰ τὸ μίαν ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων εἶναι τὴν τούτου ζωήν, οὐ δήπου γε καὶ τῇ ψυχῇ ταῦτα προσήκειν φήσομεν, ὁπόταν καθαρῶς τὴν ἰδίαν αὐτῆς ἐπισκοπῶμεν φύσιν. Εἰ γὰρ πάσης καθάπαξ τροφῆς ἐστιν ἀνενδεής, οὐκ ἂν ὀρεχθείη ποτὲ τούτων ὧν οὐδαμῶς δεῖται πρὸς τὸ εἶναι, οὔτ᾿ ἂν ὁρμήσειεν ἐπί τι τούτων οἷς μηδ᾿ ὅλως χρῆσθαι πέφυκεν· ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ἂν λυπηθείη δι᾿ ἀπορίαν χρημάτων ἢ κτημάτων, ὡς οὐδὲν αὐτῇ προσηκόντων. Εἰ δὲ καὶ φθορᾶς ἐστι κρείττων, οὐδὲν φοβεῖται τὸ παράπαν ὡς φθαρτικὸν ἑαυτῆς· οὐ γὰρ δέδοικεν οὐ λιμόν, οὐ νόσον οὐ πήρωσιν οὐ λώβην οὐ πῦρ οὐ σίδηρον, ἐπεὶ μηδὲ παθεῖν ἐκ τούτων δύναταί τι βλαβερὸν οὔτ᾿ ἀλγεινόν, οὐχ ἁπτομένων αὐτῆς τὸ παράπαν οὔτε σωμάτων οὔτε σωματικῶν δυνάμεων. Εἰ δὲ τὸ τὰ πάθη ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἰδιαζόντως προσάπτειν ἄτοπον, τὸ τὰς ἐκ τούτων ἁμαρτίας καὶ τὰς ἐπὶ ταύταις τιμωρίας ἐπὶ μόνας φέρειν τὰς ψυχὰς ὑπερβαλλόντως ἄδικον καὶ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ κρίσεως ἀνάξιον.
thought_title: Justice requires the body to share in reward and punishment
orientation: Athenagoras is arguing that God's justice requires the whole human being, body and soul together, to receive reward or punishment, and here he shows how unjust it would be to judge the soul alone for deeds in which the body was the first mover.
pass_a_gloss: For when good deeds are honored, the body will clearly be wronged from having shared with the soul in the labors over the things pursued with zeal, but not having shared in the honor over the things accomplished, and the soul often obtains pardon for certain offenses because of the body's deficiency and need, but the body itself falls away from the partnership in the things accomplished, on behalf of which it endured the labors in life. And indeed when offenses are judged, justice is not preserved for the soul, if it alone pays the penalty on behalf of the things in which it offended when the body was troubling it and dragging it toward its own appetites or movements, sometimes according to seizure and seduction, sometimes according to some more violent dragging, and at other times according to a coming together in the way of favor and care for its constitution. Or how is it not unjust for the soul to be judged by itself on behalf of things for which it has not any appetite, not movement, not impulse according to its own nature, such as lust or violence or greed or injustice and the offenses upon these? For if the majority of such evils happen from humans not mastering the troubling passions, and they are troubled by the body's deficiency and need and by the zeal and care concerning this (for on account of these is all acquisition and before this the use, and further marriage and as many actions as are in life, in which and concerning which both the offense and the not such a thing are observed), where is it just, in the things in which the body first suffers and drags the soul toward sympathy and partnership of the actions which it needs, that the soul itself be judged alone, and that the appetites and pleasures, and further fears and pains, upon which every immoderate thing is liable to judgment, have their movement from the body, but the sins from these and the punishments upon the things sinned be brought upon the soul alone, which neither needs any such thing nor desires nor fears or suffers any such thing by itself such as a human being is by nature disposed to suffer? But even if we posit that the passions are not of the body alone but of the human being, saying correctly because the life of this is one from both, we will not surely say that these belong also to the soul, whenever we examine purely its own nature. For if it is completely without need of all food, it would never desire those things which it in no way needs for being, nor would it rush toward any of those things which it is by nature disposed not to use at all; but neither would it be pained through lack of money or possessions, as these in no way belong to it. And if it is also superior to corruption, it fears nothing at all as destructive of itself; for it does not fear hunger, not disease, not mutilation, not outrage, not fire, not iron, since it cannot suffer from these anything harmful or painful, as neither bodies nor bodily powers touch it at all. And if attaching the passions to souls as proper to them is absurd, bringing the sins from these and the punishments upon them upon the souls alone is surpassingly unjust and unworthy of the judgment of God.

choices.why: Keeps the two distinct violent acts named by the objectors' scenario, preserving the legal flavor of the offenses.

choices.term: ἐν χάριτος μέρει καὶ θεραπείας τῆς τούτου συστάσεως
choices.english: in the part of favor and care of its constitution
choices.why: Renders the dative phrase literally to show the body's offenses can arise from tending to its own constitution, not only from violent dragging.
rejected: as a favor and care for its constitution
by way of gratifying and tending its constitution

choices.why: Preserves the compound's force: the body is the first to be affected, before the soul is drawn in.
Keeps the superlative adverb's intensity, matching the rhetorical climax of the section.

choices.english: unworthy of the judgment of God
choices.why: Uses the glossary term 'judgment' for κρίσις and keeps the genitive construction explicit.

pass_b_english: For when good deeds are honored, the body will clearly be wronged: it shared with the soul in the labors spent on what was pursued, but it does not share in the honor given for what was accomplished. The soul often receives pardon for certain offenses because of the body's lack and need, yet the body itself is shut out from sharing in the rewards for the good deeds—rewards for which it bore the labors together with the soul during life.

And further, when offenses are judged, justice is not preserved for the soul if it alone pays the penalty for what it did wrong when the body was troubling it and dragging it toward its own appetites or movements—sometimes toward seizure and theft, sometimes toward a more violent pulling, and at other times toward a coming together in the way of favor and care for its constitution.

Or how is it not unjust for the soul to be judged by itself for things for which it has no appetite, no movement, no impulse at all according to its own nature—such as lust, violence, greed, injustice, and the wrongs that follow from these? For if most such evils arise because human beings do not master the passions that trouble them, and they are troubled by the body's lack and need and by the effort and care devoted to it—since for the sake of these come all possessions and, before possessions, their use, and also marriage and all the actions of life, in which and around which both what is faulty and what is not are observed—where is the justice in this: the body first suffers and drags the soul into sympathy and partnership in the actions it needs, yet the soul alone is judged? The appetites and pleasures, and also fears and griefs—on which every excess is liable to punishment—have their movement from the body, but the sins arising from these and the punishments for the sins are carried to the soul alone, which neither needs any such thing nor desires it nor fears or suffers anything of the sort by itself, the sort of thing a human being naturally suffers.

But even if we grant that the passions belong not to the body alone but to the human being—and we say this rightly, because his life is one made from both—we certainly will not say that these things belong to the soul, whenever we examine its own nature purely. For if it is entirely without need of all food, it would never desire those things it in no way needs for its existence, nor would it set out toward any of those things it is not at all naturally suited to use. Nor would it grieve over a lack of money or possessions, since these do not belong to it at all.

And if it is superior to corruption, it fears nothing whatever as destructive of itself. For it does not fear hunger, disease, mutilation, injury, fire, or iron, since it cannot suffer anything harmful or painful from these; neither bodies nor bodily powers touch it at all.

But if attaching the passions to souls as proper to them is absurd, then carrying the sins that come from these and the punishments for them to the souls alone is surpassingly unjust and unworthy of the judgment of God.

problems.why: 'Theft' for κλοπήν is wrong; context requires 'seduction' or 'deception', not theft.

problems.quote: convergence in the part of favor and care of its constitution
problems.source_quote: κατὰ συνδρομὴν ἐν χάριτος μέρει καὶ θεραπείας τῆς τούτου συστάσεως
problems.why: Unintelligible rendering; 'convergence in the part of favor' is gibberish.
problems.fix: a coming together in the way of favor and care for its constitution
problems.ruling: συνδρομὴν ἐν χάριτος μέρει καὶ θεραπείας τῆς τούτου συστάσεως is rendered unintelligibly; meaning is lost.

problems.quote: convergence in the part of favor and care of its constitution
problems.source_quote: κατὰ συνδρομὴν ἐν χάριτος μέρει καὶ θεραπείας τῆς τούτου συστάσεως
problems.why: This phrase is incomprehensible to a modern reader.
problems.fix: a joint response, as a favor and to care for its constitution
problems.ruling: Duplicate of #2; same unintelligible rendering of συνδρομὴν ἐν χάριτος μέρει... loses meaning.

problems.quote: attaching the passions to souls in a special way
problems.source_quote: τὸ τὰ πάθη ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἰδιαζόντως προσάπτειν
problems.why: 'In a special way' mistranslates ἰδιαζόντως; here it means 'as proper to' or 'as belonging peculiarly to', not 'in a special way'.
problems.fix: attaching the passions to souls as proper to them
problems.ruling: ἰδιαζόντως means 'as proper/peculiar to'; 'in a special way' misleads reader about the argument's core distinction.

last_rejected.why: συναρπαγή means 'snatching away, rape, seduction' not 'seizure'; κλοπή means 'theft' but context suggests 'secret fraud' or 'stealth'.
last_rejected.ruling: συναρπαγή ('snatching/seizure') and κλοπή ('theft') are standard meanings; 'seizure and theft' is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: his life is one made from both
last_rejected.source_quote: μίαν ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων εἶναι τὴν τούτου ζωήν
last_rejected.why: τούτου refers to 'the human being' (ἀνθρώπου), not 'his'; and 'made from both' obscures that the life is one single life of both together.
last_rejected.fix: the life of the human being is one from both
last_rejected.ruling: τοῦτου refers to ἀνθρώπου; 'his life' = the human being's life. 'One made from both' captures μίαν ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων adequately.
